title: Hacker Used Chinese-Developed A.I. Tool to Target South Korean Banks, CrowdStrike Says
source_used: The Register (read in full) and Infosecurity Magazine (read in full); both report CrowdStrike's analysis. The New York Times original returned HTTP 403.
key_facts: CrowdStrike published an analysis on 7 Oct 2026 of attacks on South Korean financial institutions (The Register: report published Wednesday; Infosecurity Magazine: blog of 7 Oct).
It says a suspected China-based, Chinese-speaking, financially motivated attacker (moderate confidence) ran the campaign from late September to early October 2026.
The attacker used ARTEX, a recently released open-source agentic penetration-testing tool developed in China, together with Anthropic's Claude Code.

Per Infosecurity Magazine, the ARTEX instance used DeepSeek v4.1-flash as its main model, with GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6 added for extra Claude Code sessions; the attacker also asked Claude to find Korean Telegram groups that buy stolen data.

Exposed AI session logs on an attacker-linked server held a resume-writing request naming 'YY', a Chinese university and a location in Guangdong, with conflicting ages; CrowdStrike thinks these likely belong to the attacker but cannot prove it.

At least five lenders were affected (Shinhan, KB Kookmin, Hana, Yegaram Savings, BNK Busan, per The Korea Times via The Register); Shinhan reported about 25,000 customers affected, KB Kookmin 119 and Hana 89.
Police are investigating whether one person or an organised group is responsible; lawmakers plan to summon five bank heads to a 19 Oct parliamentary audit.
quote_evidence: The researchers found references to YY in AI sessions associated with activity involving ARTEX, a recently released open source penetration-testing tool developed in China and used in the attacks alongside Claude Code.
CrowdStrike considers the details likely to belong to the attacker but says it cannot definitively establish that connection.
Police are investigating whether an individual or an organized group carried out the attacks.
why_it_matters_hint: A security firm links a bank-data theft campaign to commercial AI coding tools and a Chinese open-source hacking agent, but the attribution is the firm's own assessment at moderate confidence.
event_date: Campaign late Sep to early Oct 2026; CrowdStrike report 7 Oct 2026; press coverage 8 Oct 2026
notes: NYT page blocked (403). Read The Register and Infosecurity Magazine instead. Infosecurity says Shinhan 25,000 and Yegaram 40,000 affected (citing The Straits Times); The Register gives Shinhan 25,000, KB Kookmin 119, Hana 89. Reuters (read in C12-08) says CrowdStrike judged the attacker probably could not have run the campaign without AI. A Global Times headline (seen, not read) says China's foreign ministry rejected CrowdStrike's claims.
